nodes.label: Amrita Devi Bishnoi and Bishnoi Community
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Bishnois of western Rajasthan (near Thar desert) have conserved forests and wildlife as a religious tenet for centuries. In 1731, Amrita Devi Bishnoi sacrificed her life along with 363 others to protect khejri trees in Khejrali village near Jodhpur. Government of India instituted the 'Amrita Devi Bishnoi National Award for Wildlife Conservation' in her memory. Their philosophy: all living things have a right to survive and share resources.

nodes.label: Cell
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms, first observed in cork by Robert Hooke in 1665. Cells are assembled to make the body of every organism, analogous to bricks in a building. They vary in shape, size, and number across organisms.

nodes.label: Cell Membrane (Plasma Membrane)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A porous membrane that separates cells from one another and from the surrounding medium. It encloses the cytoplasm and nucleus, allows movement of substances both inward and outward, and provides shape to animal cells. Present in both plant and animal cells.

nodes.label: Cell Wall
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An additional thick layer outside the cell membrane found only in plant cells and bacterial cells, absent in animal cells. It provides shape, rigidity, and protection against temperature variations, wind, and atmospheric moisture. Plants need this protection because they cannot move.

nodes.label: Cytoplasm
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The jelly-like substance present between the cell membrane and the nucleus. It contains various organelles including mitochondria, Golgi bodies, and ribosomes. Together with the nucleus, the cytoplasm constitutes protoplasm, the living substance of the cell.

nodes.label: Nucleus
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An important spherical component located in the centre of the cell, separated from cytoplasm by a nuclear membrane. Contains chromosomes carrying genes for inheritance. Acts as the control centre of cell activities. Contains a smaller body called nucleolus.

nodes.label: Gene
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The unit of inheritance in living organisms that controls the transfer of hereditary characteristics from parents to offspring. Different combinations of genes from parents result in different characteristics such as eye colour, hair type, and other traits.

nodes.label: Eukaryotic Cell
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Cells with a well-organised nucleus surrounded by a nuclear membrane. Found in all organisms other than bacteria and blue-green algae. The term comes from eu (true) and karyon (nucleus). Generally larger (5-100 micrometres) and contain membrane-bound organelles.

nodes.label: Unicellular Organisms
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Organisms made up of a single cell that performs all necessary life functions including digestion, respiration, excretion, growth, and reproduction. Examples include Amoeba (which changes shape using pseudopodia) and Paramecium.

nodes.label: Multicellular Organisms
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Organisms made of more than one cell, with billions or trillions of cells that vary in shape and size. Different groups of cells perform specialised functions, forming tissues, which form organs. Every multicellular organism begins life as a single fertilised egg cell.

nodes.label: Tissue
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A group of similar cells performing a specific function. Tissues in turn form organs. In multicellular organisms, specialised cells form different tissues that carry out functions which a single cell performs alone in unicellular organisms.

nodes.label: Vacuole
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Blank-looking structures in the cytoplasm that store substances. Plant cells have a single large central vacuole, while animal cells have much smaller vacuoles. Their size is one of the distinguishing features between plant and animal cells.

nodes.label: Chloroplast
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Green-coloured plastids found only in plant cells, containing the green pigment chlorophyll essential for photosynthesis. They provide the green colour to leaves. Plastids of different colours are scattered in the cytoplasm of leaf cells.

nodes.label: Robert Hooke
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: English scientist who in 1665 first observed cells by examining thin slices of cork under a simple magnifying device. He coined the term 'cell' for the partitioned box-like compartments he saw, which resembled a honeycomb. What he observed were actually dead cells.

nodes.label: Cell Theory
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Proposed by Schleiden and Schwann, stating that all living organisms are composed of cells, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells (added later by Virchow). The cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit of all living organisms.

nodes.label: Plasma Membrane
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The outermost covering of the cell that separates it from the external environment. Made of lipids and proteins, it is selectively permeable, allowing only certain substances to pass through. Controls movement of substances in and out of the cell through osmosis and diffusion.

nodes.label: Osmosis
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The movement of water molecules from a region of higher water concentration to a region of lower water concentration through a selectively permeable membrane. Cells in hypertonic solutions shrink (plasmolysis), in hypotonic solutions they swell. Critical for water absorption by plant roots.

nodes.label: Mitochondria
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Double membrane-bound organelles known as the powerhouse of the cell. They perform cellular respiration, breaking down glucose to release ATP (energy currency). The inner membrane is deeply folded (cristae) to increase surface area. They have their own DNA and ribosomes, suggesting they were once independent organisms.

nodes.label: Plastids
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Double membrane-bound organelles found only in plant cells. Chloroplasts (green, contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis), chromoplasts (coloured, give flowers and fruits colour), and leucoplasts (white/colourless, store starch, oils, and protein). Like mitochondria, they have their own DNA and ribosomes.

nodes.label: Vacuoles
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Storage sacs for solid or liquid contents. Plant cells have large central vacuoles providing turgidity and rigidity, storing amino acids, sugars, proteins, and waste. Animal cells have small vacuoles. In Amoeba, food vacuole contains food and contractile vacuole expels excess water.

nodes.label: Nuclear Membrane
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A double-layered membrane surrounding the nucleus, with pores allowing transfer of material between nucleus and cytoplasm. Its presence distinguishes eukaryotic cells from prokaryotic cells where nuclear material is not membrane-bound.

nodes.label: Chromatin Material
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Thread-like material in the nucleus made of DNA and protein. During cell division, chromatin condenses into chromosomes. DNA carries genetic information for inheritance. Functional segments of DNA are called genes, which determine the characteristics of organisms.

nodes.label: ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The energy currency of the cell, produced mainly in mitochondria during cellular respiration. ATP stores and releases energy for all cellular activities including muscle contraction, nerve impulse transmission, protein synthesis, and active transport across membranes.

nodes.label: Cell Division
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The process by which a cell divides to form new cells. Essential for growth, repair, and reproduction. During division, chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes. The division of the nucleus is followed by division of the cytoplasm.

nodes.label: Plant Tissues
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Two main types: meristematic (dividing tissue in growing regions) and permanent (derived from meristematic tissue, lost ability to divide). Plants have more dead cells and tissues compared to animals because they do not move and need structural support through rigid cell walls.

nodes.label: Meristematic Tissue
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Dividing tissue found in growing regions of plants. Cells are small, thin-walled, with dense cytoplasm and prominent nuclei, lacking vacuoles. Three types based on location: apical (tips of roots and shoots), lateral (girth increase), and intercalary (at base of leaves, for length growth in grasses).

nodes.label: Permanent Tissue
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Formed when meristematic tissue cells lose the ability to divide and take up permanent shape, size, and function. Classified as simple tissue (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) and complex tissue (xylem, phloem). The process of differentiation transforms meristematic cells into permanent tissues.

nodes.label: Parenchyma
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Simple permanent tissue with thin cell walls, living cells, and large intercellular spaces. Stores food, provides support, and when containing chlorophyll is called chlorenchyma (performs photosynthesis). Aerenchyma (with large air cavities) provides buoyancy in aquatic plants.

nodes.label: Animal Tissues
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Four main types: epithelial (covering/lining), connective (support and binding), muscular (movement), and nervous (stimulus response). Unlike plants, animals have more living cells as they need rapid movement and active metabolic processes.

nodes.label: Epithelial Tissue
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Covering and protective tissue forming the outermost layer of skin and lining internal organs. Types: squamous (flat, skin, oesophagus), cuboidal (kidney tubules, salivary glands), columnar (intestine), ciliated (respiratory tract, oviducts), and glandular (secretory, in glands).

nodes.label: Connective Tissue
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Tissue that binds and supports other tissues. Types: areolar (filler between organs), adipose (stores fat, insulation), bone (hard, calcium phosphate matrix), cartilage (flexible, nose and ears), tendon (connects muscle to bone), ligament (connects bone to bone), blood (fluid connective tissue).

nodes.label: Muscle Tissue
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Tissue responsible for movement, made of elongated cells called muscle fibres. Three types: striated/voluntary (skeletal, striped, attached to bones), unstriated/involuntary (smooth, in alimentary canal, iris), and cardiac (heart, striped but involuntary, branched, rhythmic contraction throughout life).

nodes.label: Nervous Tissue
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Tissue that receives stimuli and transmits nerve impulses rapidly. Made of neurons with cell body (nucleus and cytoplasm), axon (single long process), and dendrites (short branched processes). An individual nerve cell may be up to a metre long. Brain, spinal cord, and nerves are composed of this tissue.

nodes.label: Sclerenchyma
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Simple permanent tissue with uniformly thickened cell walls made of lignin, making cells dead. Provides hardness and stiffness to plant parts. Found in the husk of coconut and hard covering of seeds. These are the cells that make plant parts hard.

nodes.label: Collenchyma
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Simple permanent tissue with irregular thickened corners providing flexibility and mechanical support to growing plants. Living cells with some intercellular spaces. Found below the epidermis of leaf stalks. Allows bending without breaking.

nodes.label: Blood
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A fluid connective tissue with a liquid matrix called plasma containing RBCs (carry oxygen), WBCs (fight disease), and platelets (blood clotting). Plasma contains proteins, salts, and hormones. Blood flows through vessels connecting all parts of the body.

nodes.label: Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion continues in uniform motion in a straight line, unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force. This defines inertia: the natural tendency of objects to resist change in their state of motion. Originally proposed by Galileo.

nodes.label: Inertia
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The natural tendency of an object to resist change in its state of rest or uniform motion. Mass is the measure of inertia: heavier objects have more inertia. Explains why passengers in a bus jerk forward when brakes are applied suddenly.

nodes.label: Newton's Second Law
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The rate of change of momentum of an object is proportional to the applied unbalanced force and takes place in the direction of the force. Mathematically: F = ma (force equals mass times acceleration). Defines the unit of force: 1 newton = 1 kg x 1 m/s^2.

nodes.label: Momentum
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The product of mass and velocity of an object (p = mv). A vector quantity with SI unit kg m/s. Explains why a heavy truck at low speed and a light bullet at high speed can both have large impact. The concept connects force with motion through Newton's second law.

nodes.label: Newton's Third Law
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. Action and reaction forces act on two different objects, not the same object. Examples: recoil of a gun, walking (pushing ground backward), swimming (pushing water backward), rocket propulsion (expelling gas).

nodes.label: Conservation of Momentum
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The total momentum of an isolated system (no external forces) remains constant before and after a collision or interaction. Derived from Newton's third law. Applied in understanding collisions, explosions, rocket propulsion, and recoil of firearms.

nodes.label: Isaac Newton
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: English physicist and mathematician (1642-1727) who formulated the three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation. His Principia Mathematica (1687) laid the foundation of classical mechanics. Also made foundational contributions to optics and calculus.

nodes.label: Mass and Weight
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Mass is the amount of matter in an object (constant everywhere, measured in kg). Weight is the gravitational force on an object (W = mg, varies with location, measured in newtons). Weight on the moon is 1/6th of weight on Earth because the moon's mass and radius are smaller.

nodes.label: Sound
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A form of energy that produces the sensation of hearing, produced by vibrating objects. Sound travels as a longitudinal wave through a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) by creating compressions and rarefactions. It cannot travel through vacuum. Speed of sound in air at 20C is about 344 m/s.

nodes.label: Longitudinal Wave
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A wave in which particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation, creating alternating compressions (high density regions) and rarefactions (low density regions). Sound waves are longitudinal. Contrasted with transverse waves where particles vibrate perpendicular to wave direction.

nodes.label: Frequency
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The number of oscillations per unit time, measured in hertz (Hz). Determines the pitch of sound. Human ear can hear frequencies between 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). Higher frequency means higher pitch. Frequency and time period are inversely related: f = 1/T.

nodes.label: Amplitude
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The maximum displacement of a medium's particles from their mean position during wave propagation. Determines the loudness of sound. Greater amplitude means louder sound. Amplitude decreases as sound moves away from the source, reducing loudness.

nodes.label: Speed of Sound
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The speed at which sound waves propagate through a medium. Speed = wavelength x frequency (v = lambda x nu). Sound travels fastest in solids (5960 m/s in steel), slower in liquids (1531 m/s in water), and slowest in gases (344 m/s in air at 20C). Increases with temperature.

nodes.label: Echo
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The repetition of sound caused by reflection of sound waves from a hard surface. To hear a distinct echo, the minimum distance between the source and reflecting surface should be 17.2 m (time gap of at least 0.1 seconds). Used in sonar, stethoscopes, and measuring distances.

nodes.label: Ultrasound
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Sound with frequency greater than 20,000 Hz (above human hearing range). Used in medical imaging (ultrasonography for pregnancy monitoring), cleaning hard-to-reach parts, detecting cracks in metals, SONAR, and breaking kidney stones (lithotripsy). Produced by quartz crystals.

nodes.label: SONAR
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Sound Navigation and Ranging, a technique using ultrasonic waves to measure the distance, direction, and speed of underwater objects. Transmitter produces ultrasonic waves, receiver detects reflected waves. Used to detect submarines, depth of sea, underwater hills, valleys, and icebergs.

nodes.label: Infrasound
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Sound with frequency below 20 Hz, below the range of human hearing. Produced by earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and some animals. Rhinoceroses communicate using infrasound. Whales and elephants also produce infrasonic sounds for long-distance communication.

nodes.label: Reflection of Sound
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Sound waves bounce off hard surfaces following the laws of reflection (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection). Applications include megaphones, hearing aids, stethoscopes, and the curved ceiling of concert halls. Multiple reflections cause reverberation in large halls.

nodes.label: Human Ear
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Auditory organ with three parts: outer ear (pinna collects sound), middle ear (three bones - hammer, anvil, stirrup amplify vibrations), and inner ear (cochlea converts vibrations to electrical signals sent to brain via auditory nerve). Eardrum vibrates at the frequency of incoming sound.

nodes.label: Wavelength
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The distance between two consecutive compressions or two consecutive rarefactions in a longitudinal wave. Denoted by lambda. Related to speed and frequency by v = lambda x nu. Measured in metres. Shorter wavelength corresponds to higher frequency and higher pitch.

nodes.label: Musical Sound vs Noise
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Musical sound is pleasant, periodic, and composed of a rich mixture of frequencies (notes). Noise is unpleasant and irregular. Quality or timbre distinguishes sounds of the same pitch and loudness from different sources. A tone is sound of single frequency, while a note is a mixture.
